items.title: Root-mean-square (rms) or Effective Value of Current and Voltage:

source_refs.note: Root-mean-square (rms) or Effective Value of Current and Voltage:: a main subheading of 17.1 Alternating Current and its Characteristics, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 87-89.

blocks.text: Root-mean- square (rms) values of current, or voltage, are a useful way of comparing alternating current, or voltage, to its equivalent direct current, or voltage. The rms values represent the direct current, or voltage, values that will produce the same heating effect, or power dissipation as the alternating current or voltage. The rms value of an alternating current is defined as:
The value of a constant current that produces the same power in a resistor as the alternating current.

blocks.title: Point to ponder!
blocks.text:
Why do high voltage power lines crackle and hiss?
The hissing sound often heard near high voltage power lines is primarily caused by corona discharge, an electrical phenomenon where the air surrounding the conductor becomes ionized due to a strong electric field. This ionization creates a discharge that can produce a visible glow, radio noise, and audible hissing or crackling sounds, particularly when the voltage exceeds the breakdown strength of the air.
The rms value of an alternating voltage is defined as:
The value of a constant voltage that produces the same power in a resistor as the alternating voltage.
So, rms current, Iᵣₘₛ is equal to 0.707 Iₒ, which is about 70% of the peak current Iₒ.

blocks.title: Example 17.1
blocks.problem: The steady direct current, or voltage that delivers the same average power in a resistor as the alternating current, or voltage. Using the graph as shown in the figure and the equation for alternating current, calculate the value of the current at a time 0.67 s.
steps:
We know that for AC circuits;
I = Iₒ sin (ωt) and ω = 2π/T

The time period T is the time taken for one full cycle, and peak current Iₒ from the graph are:
T = 0.10 s and Iₒ = 17 A

Using the equation I = Iₒ sin (ωt)
As ω = 2π/T, therefore, I = Iₒ sin (2π/T) t

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: 2 × 3.14 × 0.67 s / 0.1 s = 42.1 is an angle in radians, not 42° (and sin 42° would be 0.669, not 0.917). In radians: t/T = 6.7, so the current has made 6 full cycles plus 0.7 of a cycle (4.40 rad = 252°); sin 252° = −0.951, so I = 17 A × (−0.951) ≈ −16.2 A, i.e. 16.2 A in the negative direction.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text:
How can you tell if a current is alternating?
Step 1: Determine the direction of the electric current.
Step 2: Determine whether the current's direction changes or stays the same.
Step 3: If the current periodically reverses direction, it is alternating current. If the current flows in a single direction, it is direct current.
